summary: Sets out the administrative policies for running remote printer facilities in the tpc.int subdomain. It covers ways to recover costs and discusses auditing, security, and denial of access.

eli5.summary: A shared printer needs house rules. This memo lists who pays, who is allowed to use it, and how to keep things safe.

subtitle: Rules for running shared fax service through the Internet.

tldr.problem: Early remote printing services let people send email to fax machines, but operators needed guidelines on how to recover costs and protect privacy when most users were unknown.
tldr.mechanism: Define three business models (community service, commercial subscription, sponsored), auditing requirements, privacy rules, and access control policies for remote printer operators.
tldr.outcome: Remote printing was an early bridge between email and fax communities, but this experimental infrastructure has largely faded as fax itself became less central to business communication.

today: RFC 1529 is informational. Remote printing was an experimental service to bridge email and fax; the service has faded as fax became less central to business communication.

sections.title: The Service
sections.content:
Remote printing in the tpc.int subdomain bridges email and G3-compatible facsimile (fax) machines. A user sends an email to an address that includes a telephone number—for example, user+12015551234@remote-printer.example.com. The Internet infrastructure routes the message to a remote printer server, which dials the fax number and images the email on the receiving fax machine, then sends back an acknowledgement.

This allows people with email to reach people with only fax, and organizations to accept faxes without paper. The challenge is that the initiator of a fax is unknown and cannot be billed in advance, yet the service consumes resources on the sender's Internet connection and the telephone network.
sections.eli5: You could email a fax machine. A server would dial the number and print your email as a fax. These rules say how to pay for it and keep everyone's privacy.

sections.title: Three Cost Models
sections.content:
The RFC defines three ways to recover the cost of running a remote printer server.

The Community Library model treats remote printing as a public service, like a library. An organization registers to serve a region for free, absorbing the cost as a community contribution.

The Neighborhood Grocery model is commercial: a service bureau contracts with individual fax owners to register their numbers, similar to a phone listing service. Cost recovery may come from the fax owner, the user, or both.

The Local Newspaper model recovers costs from a sponsor. The service shows up to one-third of the cover sheet as sponsorship and allows up to 250 bytes of acknowledgement text in the reply, clearly marked as a paid advertisement if money changed hands.
sections.eli5: Free service (like a library), paid service to the fax owner (like a phone book), or paid service with ads (like a newspaper).

sections.title: Auditing and Access Control
sections.content:
Remote printer servers should maintain a log for audit and security, recording at most: the date received, the From and Message-ID fields from the email, the message size, the fax telephone number, call duration, and G3-related metadata. Such logs are not to be divulged except by legal requirement, and never for marketing lists.

Operators may deny access based on the message source (sender) if abuse or legal reasons require it, and must send a notification explaining the policy violated. However, they may not deny access based on the destination (the fax number being called), as that would let them filter which fax machines could be reached. If an operator finds a destination inappropriate, it should re-register to exclude that range.
sections.eli5: Keep a log of who sent what, but only for catching trouble. Never sell the list. You can block a bad sender but not a bad fax number.
